lesson.title: The Strongest Handshake Between Molecules
lesson.summary: Hydrogen bonding is an especially strong form of dipole-dipole attraction that occurs when hydrogen, bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom, is attracted to a lone pair on a neighboring electronegative atom.
lesson.body:
Hydrogen bonding is not a new category of force so much as an unusually strong, special case of the dipole-dipole forces already introduced. It occurs under a specific structural condition: a hydrogen atom must be covalently bonded to one of just three small, highly electronegative elements, nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine, and that hydrogen must then come close to a lone pair of electrons on a nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine atom belonging to a neighboring molecule. The large electronegativity difference in bonds like O-H, N-H, or F-H pulls electron density strongly away from the hydrogen, leaving it with an unusually large partial positive charge, and because a hydrogen atom is so small, with no inner electron shell to shield its nucleus, that exposed positive charge can approach a neighboring lone pair unusually closely, producing an attraction significantly stronger than typical dipole-dipole forces between larger atoms.

Water is again the clearest illustration, and revisiting it here ties together the whole chapter. Each O-H bond is strongly polar because of the large electronegativity difference between oxygen and hydrogen, giving water its bent, polar geometry as established at the start of this chapter. Each water molecule can act as a hydrogen bond donor through its two O-H hydrogens and as a hydrogen bond acceptor through its two oxygen lone pairs, allowing every water molecule to form up to four hydrogen bonds with its neighbors at once. This extensive hydrogen bonding network is why water has a boiling point of 100 degrees Celsius, dramatically higher than expected for a molecule of its small size and low electron count; compare it with H2S, similar in shape and formula but built from sulfur instead of oxygen, which boils at about negative 60 degrees Celsius because sulfur is far less electronegative than oxygen and therefore cannot support significant hydrogen bonding.

Ammonia, NH3, and hydrogen fluoride, HF, show the same pattern for the same underlying reason. Both boil noticeably higher than the hydrides of neighboring elements in their respective periods that lack an N-H, O-H, or F-H bond, precisely because nitrogen and fluorine are electronegative enough, and hydrogen small enough, to support hydrogen bonding where phosphorus or chlorine hydrides cannot. This is the practical test for hydrogen bonding: look specifically for H bonded directly to N, O, or F, since hydrogen bonded to carbon, sulfur, or chlorine, for example, does not qualify, no matter how polar that particular bond might be, because those elements are either not electronegative enough or not small enough to produce the same concentrated effect.

Hydrogen bonding completes the intermolecular force strength ranking built across this chapter: London dispersion forces, present in all molecules and growing with polarizability, are typically weakest for small molecules; dipole-dipole forces, present in polar molecules generally, are stronger; and hydrogen bonding, the special, unusually strong dipole-dipole interaction limited to H bonded to N, O, or F, is typically strongest of the three for molecules of comparable size. As with every step in this ranking, size still matters, since a very large molecule with only dispersion forces can still exceed a small hydrogen bonding molecule in total attraction, but for molecules of similar size, hydrogen bonding reliably produces the largest boiling point and melting point elevation of any intermolecular force covered in this chapter.
